newsitem.title: UK: UK's Ashdown - rates, taxes to rise after election.
newsitem.headline: UK's Ashdown - rates, taxes to rise after election.

text.p: British interest rates and taxes will have to rise after the forthcoming election no matter which party takes power, Paddy Ashdown, leader of Britain's minority Liberal Democrats, said on Wednesday.
"The other side of the election, two things will happen whoever is Chancellor," Ashdown told reporters. They would be higher interest rates and higher rates of tax, he said.
An election must be held by May 22. Prime Minister John Major is believed to favour May 1.
"Rates will go up probably twice as much as they would have had to if we had raised them (recently)," Ashdown said.

At the last monetary meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George, Clarke decided to leave base rates unchanged at six percent. Rates have been stuck there since October 30.
Minutes from the previous meeting in January showed George strongly advised a quarter-point increase.
"In the course of the next year, if not in the middle of this year, those tax cuts that have been handed out...will have to be recovered," Ashdown added.

Turning to comments from Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind that, on balance, the government was hostile to the planned launch of a single European currency in January 1999, he said the government could not maintain any position on Europe.
"The Conservatives...are becoming the edge of Europe' party and will become the 'out-of-Europe' after the election. That is almost inevitable," Ashdown said.
He reaffirmed his commitment to invest an extra two billion pounds in education and if necessary add a penny to the basic rate of income tax, cut to 23 percent at the November budget, to pay for it.
Opposition Labour Party leader Tony Blair has pledged to put education at the heart of his policies if he takes power.

But Ashdown noted that shadow Chancellor Gordon Brown has said he would adopt the government's spending plans for the next two years. "The budget Red Book shows quite clearly in the next financial year, the budget for the Department of Education and Employment goes down by nine percent," he said.
He said the Labour Party should "put its money where its mouth is. A promise without a cost is nearly always a lie."
